title: Collateral, Health Factor, and Liquidation
objectives: Know why every DeFi loan is overcollateralized
Read and calculate Health Factor so you know your own danger line
Follow a liquidation bot through the trade and see where its profit comes from
Understand why the liquidation threshold sits above max LTV

steps.title: Why Overcollateralization is Required
steps.body:
A Web3 wallet is pseudonymous — a string of characters with no name, no ID, no credit file. A protocol has no courthouse to sue you in and no collection agency to call. That missing legal safety net is exactly why every DeFi loan is overcollateralized.

Think of it as a vending machine. It will not hand you a snack on a promise to pay later. Your <Term id="collateral">collateral</Term> has to already be inside the machine before the flap opens.

- To borrow $1,000 of USDC you deposit more than $1,000 of volatile crypto — $1,500 of SOL, say.
- The contract holds that SOL in escrow. You still own it, but you cannot withdraw it while the debt is open.
- The $500 of cushion above your debt is the lender's protection against SOL suddenly dropping.

Why the extra? If SOL crashed the instant you borrowed, the protocol would already hold more value than you owe and could stay whole without a lawyer or a credit score. That surplus is not a fee. It is what lets a bot-run, permissionless system remain solvent.

The gap between what you may borrow and what you deposited is your <Term id="ltv">LTV</Term>, and the moment your collateral drifts too close to your debt, the protocol watches a single number to decide whether you are still safe.

steps.title: The Vital Metric: Health Factor
steps.body:
All of that collapses into one number the protocol recalculates constantly: your <Term id="health_factor">Health Factor</Term>. It answers a single question — if your collateral were liquidated right now, would the recovered value still cover the debt with room to spare?

`Health Factor = (Collateral Value × Liquidation Threshold) / Borrowed Debt`

Reading it like a dashboard gauge:

- **HF above 1.5.** Safe. Your collateral could lose a large chunk of value and you would still be covered.
- **HF between 1.0 and 1.3.** Danger zone. One bad candle can push you under, so top up or repay.
- **HF below 1.0.** Liquidatable. The contract now lets anyone repay part of your loan and seize your collateral.

Why multiply by the **liquidation threshold** rather than the raw collateral value? Because the protocol deliberately counts your collateral for less than its market price. If your <Term id="ltv">LTV</Term> lets you borrow against 70% of your SOL, the threshold might sit at 80%. That gap is breathing room, not a bug.

Worked example: you deposit $2,000 of SOL at an 80% threshold and borrow $1,000. HF = ($2,000 × 0.80) / $1,000 = 1.60. SOL falls 30%, collateral is now $1,400, and HF = ($1,400 × 0.80) / $1,000 = 1.12 — the danger zone. It slips once more to $1,200 and HF hits 0.96. The <Term id="liquidation">liquidation</Term> machinery switches on.

steps.title: Under the Hood: How Liquidator Bots Profit
steps.body:
The protocol almost never liquidates you itself. It cannot watch every position at once and it does not want to hold risky assets. Instead it posts a bounty: anyone who keeps the system solvent may profit. Those anyone-people are liquidator bots, and their reward is the liquidation penalty.

How a liquidation executes:

- The moment your HF slips below 1.0, the contract opens a window where any bot may repay a slice of your debt — often half of it — on your behalf.
- In exchange the bot receives your collateral at a 5% to 10% discount to the price the <Term id="oracle">oracle</Term> reports. That discount is the bonus.
- The bot immediately sells the collateral on an AMM at full market price, pocketing the spread.

Follow the money. Your debt is $1,000 of USDC against $1,000 of SOL. A bot repays $500 of your USDC and, with a 10% bonus, seizes $550 worth of SOL. It sells that SOL for roughly $550 and clears about $50 of gross profit. Your debt already shrank by $500.

The penalty is real and it is yours: you lose the collateral the bot takes plus the bonus on top. That is why liquidators are not villains. They are the immune system of a lending market, and 1.0 is the threshold where it attacks. The <Term id="oracle">oracle</Term> price is the referee that decides when that line is crossed — which is also why manipulating oracles is such a prized attack in DeFi.

questions.prompt: What is the core reason DeFi loans are almost always overcollateralized?
options: Because Solana gas fees make undercollateralized loans unprofitable for validators to process
Because a 150% collateral ratio is mandated by US securities law for all on-chain lending
Because borrowers are pseudonymous, so a protocol has no legal way to pursue an unpaid debt
Because posting more collateral lets a protocol mint extra governance tokens to reward lenders
questions.explainRight: A pseudonymous wallet has no identity to sue and no credit history to price, so the only enforcement a protocol has is seizing assets already locked up. Overcollateralization replaces the legal system with arithmetic.
questions.explainWrong: Gas fees and governance rewards have nothing to do with it, and no US statute requires a 150% ratio on Solana. It is a design choice forced by the absence of legal recourse, not a regulatory rule.

questions.prompt: Two borrowers each borrow $1,000 of USDC against SOL with the same 80% liquidation threshold. Borrower A deposited $3,000 of SOL; Borrower B deposited $1,200. Which position is safer against a price crash, and why?
options: Borrower B, because a smaller collateral value means the oracle refreshes it less often
Borrower A, because the larger collateral cushion produces a higher Health Factor for the same debt
They are equally safe because both borrowers owe exactly the same $1,000 of debt
Borrower B, because liquidators only target positions holding more than $2,000 of collateral
questions.explainRight: Health Factor scales with collateral relative to debt. Borrower A starts at ($3,000 × 0.80) / $1,000 = 2.40; Borrower B starts at ($1,200 × 0.80) / $1,000 = 0.96 — already liquidatable. More cushion means a bigger price fall before HF crosses 1.0.
questions.explainWrong: Look past the identical $1,000 debt and plug in the collateral. Oracle refresh rate plays no role, and liquidators seize any qualifying position regardless of size. The ratio of collateral to debt is what determines safety.

questions.prompt: A borrower's Health Factor falls to 1.15 during a market crash. Which single action most directly raises it back toward safety?
options: Switching to a faster RPC endpoint so prices refresh more frequently
Borrowing more USDC and swapping it into high-yield tokens to grow the position
Doing nothing, because Health Factor self-corrects at the next Solana epoch
Depositing additional collateral or repaying part of the outstanding debt
questions.explainRight: HF is effectively collateral value divided by debt, so you can only move it by changing one of those two numbers. Adding collateral raises the numerator; repaying debt lowers the denominator. Both lift HF immediately, and acting early is far cheaper than being liquidated.
questions.explainWrong: Remember the formula. A faster RPC endpoint changes nothing about your ratio, borrowing more makes it worse, and HF is not a network-level value that resets at epoch boundaries.

questions.prompt: You deposit $2,000 of SOL with an 80% liquidation threshold and borrow $1,000 USDC, giving an initial HF of 1.60. SOL then falls 30%. What is your new Health Factor?
questions.explainRight: A 30% drop takes $2,000 of collateral to $1,400. Then HF = ($1,400 × 0.80) / $1,000 = 1.12. Two steps: reprice the collateral, then apply the threshold, then divide by unchanged debt.
questions.explainWrong: Work it in order — reprice to $1,400, apply the 80% threshold to get $1,120, divide by the still-$1,000 debt. Answers like 1.60 forget the crash; 0.90 and 1.28 come from applying the percentage at the wrong step.

questions.prompt: Why do liquidator bots usually sell the seized collateral immediately on an AMM rather than holding it?
options: Because the law requires seized collateral to be converted into stablecoins within one block
Because AMMs pay liquidators a special protocol grant for every liquidation they process
Because their profit is the gap between the discounted oracle valuation and the market price, so holding only adds price risk with no extra reward
Because the seized collateral is encrypted and only an AMM holds the key that releases it
questions.explainRight: The edge is buying collateral below market via the bonus and flipping it at market — a locked-in spread. Holding the volatile collateral re-exposes the bot to the very price move that triggered the liquidation.
questions.explainWrong: There is no legal one-block rule, no special grant, and no cryptographic gate. Liquidators sell instantly because their business is capturing the discount, not taking directional bets on SOL.

questions.prompt: A price oracle briefly reports SOL 20% lower for 30 seconds due to a manipulation attempt, even though the true market price never moved. Both the liquidator bots and the protocol's risk engine read that same oracle. What is the most accurate consequence for an otherwise healthy borrower?
options: Nothing happens, because liquidations always use a full-day average price and ignore short spikes
The borrower can be liquidated if their HF dips below 1.0 on that manipulated reading, which is exactly why robust protocols price collateral with time-weighted averages instead of a single moment
Manipulation is impossible because oracles are run by validators who are economically unable to lie
The borrower's debt is automatically frozen for 30 seconds until the price recovers
questions.explainRight: If the oracle is a single instantaneous reading, a 30-second dip can drag HF under 1.0 and trigger real liquidations even though the true price never moved. That is precisely why serious protocols use time-weighted averages or multiple sources — to smooth out flash spikes.
questions.explainWrong: The danger is real: an instantaneous oracle can be pushed under a borrower's safety line for a few seconds, and liquidations on that print are final. Not all protocols use day-long averages, and debt is never frozen mid-crash.

questions.prompt: Why is the liquidation threshold set higher than the maximum LTV a borrower can use?
options: Because the threshold is a fee charged only to borrowers who never repay their loan
Because the LTV is set by the DAO while the threshold is hard-coded into Solana's runtime
Because borrowers demanded a second, redundant ratio to confuse competing lending protocols
Because the gap lets a position be liquidated while the collateral still fully covers the debt, so a small price dip cannot turn into a loss for lenders
questions.explainRight: LTV caps how much you can borrow at entry; the higher threshold defines when you get liquidated. That buffer is deliberate — it ensures that when HF hits 1.0 your collateral still covers the debt plus the liquidator's bonus, so the protocol never eats a shortfall.
questions.explainWrong: The gap is a solvency design, not a fee or a governance quirk. Because the threshold sits above the LTV, a position that reaches liquidation still holds enough to cover the debt and pay the bonus.
